Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday to elect their next president

Brazilians will vote for their next president on Sunday after neither the incumbent left-wing candidate, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, nor his right-wing opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, garnered a majority of the votes in the election’s first round earlier this month. Bolsonaro, who has the support of President Donald Trump, is the slight favorite heading into Sunday’s runoff, with him leading by roughly one percentage point in the most recent polls released on Saturday, according to Reuters. The two candidates finalized the arguments of their campaigns on Saturday, as Lula marched along Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beach, while Bolsonaro campaigned in a key battleground state.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that Lula won the election with 51.77% of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48.23%, securing a fourth term, while FOX News states that Lula won 51.8% of the vote, defeating Bolsonaro by nearly 4.4 million votes. The Washington Examiner and Newsweek both mention that Bolsonaro led by about one percentage point in the most recent polls, but Newsweek provides specific poll numbers showing a dead heat. The Guardian and Mother Jones do not mention the final vote totals, instead focusing on the campaign and public sentiment. The Guardian also notes that Lula’s campaign organized a large rally on Copacabana beach, while the Washington Examiner and FOX News describe Lula’s campaign activities without mentioning the rally. Mother Jones includes details about the Kennedy family’s wedding and an inflatable missile rally, which are not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · ABC News · Mother Jones · FOX News · The Guardian · Newsweek

Trump, Justice Department escalate fight over Alaska Senate ballot

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the results of its U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. The lawsuit argues that a second candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, whose name closely resembles that of the incumbent, could confuse voters and siphon support from Sullivan. Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the lawsuit, stating it aims to preserve ballots and allow state officials to assess potential voter confusion. The case has drawn criticism from election experts and advocacy groups, who argue the legal claim is weak and represents an unprecedented federal intervention.

The Alaska Supreme Court previously ruled that Dan J. Sullivan should remain on the ballot, and state election officials have not removed him despite concerns about voter confusion. A recent poll cited in the source material placed Peltola at 49% and Sullivan at 46%, though the methodology and margin of error were not provided. Trump claimed during a news conference that the challenger had received about 2.5 to 3 percentage points in the primary and could receive a similar share in the general election. He also accused Democrats of using the candidate to interfere in the election without offering evidence.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News reports that Trump recommended the Justice Department examine Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy, while The Guardian and The Hill state that Trump claimed to have directed the DOJ to file the lawsuit. The Free Press and Axios describe the second candidate as having donated to Peltola and working with a Democratic strategist, a detail not included in Straight Arrow News. The Guardian and The Hill note that legal experts have criticized the lawsuit as legally weak, while Straight Arrow News and The Free Press mention Common Cause and the ACLU opposing the suit. The Guardian and The Hill also include quotes from law professors Derek Mueller and Richard H Pildes, which are absent from other accounts.

Sources Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · The Free Press · Axios · Newsweek · The Hill

Venezuela opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to country

Venezuela opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to her home country after nearly a year in exile, according to multiple accounts. She announced her arrival on social media, writing, “I am here. With you.” Her return was marked by enthusiastic support from Venezuelans, with supporters gathering to greet her at a church in Barquisimeto, west of Caracas. Machado, who had been barred from exiting Venezuela by the Maduro government, had previously attempted to return multiple times but was denied entry. She had fled the country in December 2025 under the cover of darkness to accept the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize in Norway. Her return was described by her senior adviser, David Smoalnsky, as “a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections.”

Machado’s return coincided with the ongoing leadership of interim President Delcy Rodríguez, a Maduro ally who was backed by the Trump administration after the U.S. military deposed Maduro in January 2026. Rodríguez has remained in office beyond her authorized term, with no election scheduled. Machado’s return was also noted by U.S. President Donald Trump, who said, “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe. She’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed Machado’s return was “the direct result of the U.S. supported reconciliation talks.”

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the Trump administration had reportedly opposed Machado’s return, believing her presence would complicate the relationship with interim president Delcy Rodríguez. This claim is not present in the other accounts. The BBC and Straight Arrow News mention that Machado’s return was contingent on approval from the Trump administration, while CBS News and NPR do not specify this condition. The Guardian also states that Machado took eight hours to reach Caracas due to massive crowds, a detail not included in other accounts. The Christian Science Monitor notes that Machado was briefly detained in January 2025, a detail not mentioned in the BBC or NPR accounts.

Sources CBS News · Christian Science Monitor · BBC · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · NPR

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Obama rips Trump for tariffs and White House renovations as he touts El-Sayed in Detroit

Former President Barack Obama criticized President Donald Trump during a Detroit rally on Saturday, focusing on Trump’s trade policies, White House renovations, and alleged corruption. Obama mocked Trump’s focus on redecorating the White House, suggesting he should be on HGTV, and accused the administration of a “culture that’s set at the top” of corruption. He also took aim at Trump’s trade war with Canada, calling it a conflict with “that historical adversary of ours.” Obama endorsed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, framing the race as an “inflection point” for change in Michigan. El-Sayed, who has a history of criticizing Obama, praised the former president’s work on healthcare and called their shared experiences as sons of African immigrants a source of inspiration.

Obama’s remarks were part of a broader campaign push for El-Sayed, who faces Republican Mike Rogers, a Trump-endorsed candidate. The rally coincided with Trump’s planned visit to Michigan, where he would campaign for Rogers. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne County health official, won his party’s primary after defeating moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens. Obama’s support for El-Sayed marked his first public endorsement of the candidate during the midterms.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Guardian both describe Obama’s criticism of Trump’s White House renovations and his mocking of the administration’s alleged corruption. The Washington Examiner and The Intercept do not mention these specific remarks. The Straight Arrow News and The Free Press do not detail Obama’s comments on the White House renovations or the alleged corruption. The Straight Arrow News focuses more on the broader political context of the race, while The Intercept highlights internal Democratic Party tensions and the DSA’s role in the primary. The Washington Examiner mentions Bernie Sanders’ involvement in the rally but does not describe Obama’s specific criticisms of Trump. The Free Press does not mention the White House renovations or the alleged corruption, focusing instead on the broader Democratic case for El-Sayed.

Sources New York Post · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · The Intercept · The Free Press

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Serbian Nationalist Leader Who Courted MAGA Just Lost in a Landslide

Serbian nationalist leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in parliamentary elections on Sunday, marking a significant political shift. The student-led opposition movement, known as the Student List, emerged from mass protests following the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. The movement, which avoided taking a firm stance on Kosovo, focused on anti-corruption and institutional reform. Vucic, who has cultivated ties to Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, faced accusations of downplaying Serbia's 1990s war crimes and using state resources for his own benefit. The election results, which saw high voter turnout, signaled a broad rejection of Vucic's rule, with the Student List projected to win between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and Axios both report that Vucic's coalition won 105 seats, while the Student List won 135-140. Axios and The Guardian mention that Vucic projected the Student List would win 135-140 seats, while CBS News states Vucic said the Students' List took around 2.2 million votes compared to his 1.7 million. Al Jazeera and The Guardian note that Vucic conceded defeat, while CBS News reports he blamed "independent media" and "European countries" for the loss. Mother Jones and Axios describe Vucic's support for Jared Kushner's hotel project, which Al Jazeera and CBS News also mention, but Al Jazeera adds that Vucic's political mentor, Aleksandar Seselj, was on his electoral list. The Guardian and CBS News mention the high voter turnout, while Mother Jones and Axios provide more detail on the election's implications for U.S.-Serbia relations.

Sources Mother Jones · Axios · NPR · Al Jazeera · The Guardian · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Peltola to reschedule Fairbanks, Bethel campaign stops after car crash

Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, announced she would reschedule her campaign events in Fairbanks and Bethel following a car crash that resulted in minor injuries. The accident occurred on Saturday, and Peltola’s campaign stated that she and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. The Fairbanks and Bethel events, originally scheduled for Sunday and Monday, will be rescheduled for later in the week. Peltola’s campaign manager, Cheryl Bruce, noted that Peltola is disappointed about the delay but remains eager to resume campaigning. The Anchorage Police Department reported a traffic collision involving Peltola’s vehicle, with the circumstances under investigation. The incident comes as Peltola faces off against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a closely contested race.

Peltola’s campaign said the crash occurred while she was traveling to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet. The crash involved another vehicle and resulted in a multi-vehicle collision. The Anchorage Police Department confirmed the crash happened around 6:55 PM on Saturday. Peltola’s family and another vehicle’s occupant were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, while a third occupant refused medical transport. The campaign stated that Peltola will resume her campaign activities on Tuesday with a stop in Homer, Alaska.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and The Guardian both mention that the Anchorage Police Department reported a traffic collision involving Peltola’s car, while The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News refer to it as a “multi-vehicle collision.” The Hill and The Guardian specify that the crash involved another car, while The Daily Wire and The New York Post mention a third vehicle involved. The Daily Wire and The New York Post refer to the third candidate as “Decoy Dan,” while The Guardian and The Hill describe him as Daniel J. Sullivan. The Daily Wire and The New York Post note that the Justice Department filed a lawsuit to block certification if Sullivan loses, while The Guardian and The Hill mention this as well but do not name the third candidate. The Straight Arrow News omits details about the third candidate and the lawsuit.

Sources The Hill · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Straight Arrow News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

California leader calls attack on alleged noncitizen voting ‘weaponizing the law’

California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, criticized the Trump administration’s efforts to challenge alleged noncitizen voting, calling it “politicizing and weaponizing the law.” He accused the Justice Department of acting at Donald Trump’s direction. Less than two weeks before the midterms, federal prosecutors asked California election officials to verify within 48 hours a list of about 20,000 ballots belonging to suspected noncitizens. The Justice Department also charged 28 foreign nationals recently, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote. California officials raised concerns that the directive could disenfranchise citizens, noting that a “high percentage” of the individuals on the list were born in the United States.

A federal appeals court expressed skepticism about the Trump administration’s lawsuit against California, questioning whether the Justice Department’s request to segregate ballots was consistent with the Elections Clause, which gives states authority over election administration. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, raised concerns about the reliability of the administration’s list of suspected noncitizens and whether the court had jurisdiction to intervene. The case is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the midterms.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, accused the Justice Department of acting at Trump’s direction and called the effort “weaponizing the law.” Al Jazeera and The Hill do not mention Bonta’s direct accusation of Trump’s direction, though all three outlets report that the Justice Department sought to segregate ballots. The Guardian and Straight Arrow News both mention that the Justice Department charged 28 foreign nationals, while Al Jazeera and The Hill do not. The Guardian and The Hill describe the list as containing 20,000 names, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News refer to it as “roughly 20,000.” The Guardian and Straight Arrow News attribute the claim that a “high percentage” of the list were born in the U.S. to California officials, while Al Jazeera and The Hill do not.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · The Hill · FOX News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Obama criticizes Trump over Iran war and economy as he campaigns for Democrats

Former President Barack Obama criticized the Trump administration for escalating the war with Iran and for driving up fuel prices during his campaign for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Obama accused Trump of causing “chaos and corruption” and blamed the conflict for rising oil and diesel prices, citing attacks on US military bases and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. He also criticized Trump’s tariffs, arguing they are making goods more expensive for American consumers.

Obama further accused Trump of enriching the wealthy and failing to address the growing national debt, which has reached $40 trillion. He also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for focusing on military culture and the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former soldier convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Meanwhile, Trump defended his policies, claiming the economy is improving and that fuel prices will eventually drop.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports Obama blamed Trump for starting the Iran war and linked it to rising fuel prices, while BBC attributes the same claims to Obama but adds that Trump acknowledged oil prices were “temporarily high.” CBS News and Just The News do not mention the Iran war or fuel prices in the same way, focusing instead on economic concerns and voter trust. The Guardian provides a broader context about the midterm elections but does not detail Obama’s specific criticisms of Trump.

Sources Al Jazeera · The Guardian · Just The News · CBS News · BBC

No source labeled right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: One thousand three hundred sexual abuse survivors receive $800 million in compensation, addressing long-term harm and restoring rights for victims.

Archdiocese of New York agrees to $800 million settlement over sexual abuse claims

The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million to settle claims brought by approximately 1,300 individuals who allege they were sexually abused by clergy members and lay workers. Jeff Anderson, a lawyer representing over 250 of the plaintiffs, stated the settlement was finalized and that all plaintiffs had agreed to it. Archbishop Ronald Hicks, in an email shared with NPR, noted the deal had not yet been signed but that an agreement had been reached with plaintiffs and their attorneys. The agreement was first reported by The New York Times.

The settlement is the second-largest in the Catholic Church related to sexual abuse claims, following the $880 million deal reached by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles in 2024. The Archdiocese of New York had previously agreed to mediation in December 2025 to settle the 1,300 sexual abuse claims and planned to raise $300 million through staff layoffs and property sales. According to Al Jazeera, each of the approximately 1,300 survivors will receive at least $250,000 from the Archdiocese of New York, with potential for more based on the severity of the abuse.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that the settlement was finalized and that all plaintiffs had agreed to it, while Al Jazeera reports that the settlement will be formally signed on November 6. NPR mentions that the agreement was first reported by The New York Times, whereas Al Jazeera attributes the story to The New York Times as well but adds that each survivor will receive at least $250,000. Al Jazeera also includes a statement from Jeff Anderson about the survivors' "unanimous agreement" and their role in bringing about a "reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability," which NPR does not mention.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera

No source labeled center or lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Pentagon drafts Iran attack plans as Tehran threatens aggressive retaliation

The U.S. military has prepared options for potential strikes against Iran following the midterm elections, according to a source familiar with the planning. The U.S. Central Command (Centcom) has developed a range of strike options, which are being presented to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. President Trump has not ruled out military action against Iran, with some analysts suggesting a likely return to strikes after the November midterms. The Trump administration is under pressure to secure concessions from Iran amid stalled diplomatic talks, with some officials expressing frustration over the lack of progress. The military is also preparing for potential involvement from Israeli forces, which could shift the focus of strikes toward civilian and energy infrastructure.

The intelligence community has warned that Iran has increased its efforts to target U.S. personnel abroad, with plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton informed Secretary of State Marco Rubio of the threat in an unclassified memo, which was obtained by multiple outlets. The memo did not specify targets or countries outside the Middle East, nor did it indicate whether attacks were imminent. The warning comes as the State Department reduces staffing at several embassies in the region, citing threats from Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen. The administration is also considering renewed military strikes against Iran, with some officials suggesting the possibility of another operation similar to the previous campaign.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill reports that the Pentagon has drafted attack plans and that Centcom has strike options ready for presentation to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, while The Daily Wire, New York Post, CBS News, Axios, and FOX News focus on the intelligence warning about Iranian plots against U.S. personnel. The Hill attributes the planning to Centcom and mentions the involvement of Gregory Brew and Harrison Mann, while the other outlets do not mention these individuals. The Daily Wire and New York Post note that the memo did not identify specific targets or countries outside the Middle East, whereas The Hill does not mention this detail. The Hill also states that the Pentagon has not responded to its request for comment, while the other outlets do not mention this.

Sources The Hill · The Daily Wire · New York Post · CBS News · Axios · FOX News

Paris Shops Damaged, Protests Escalate Amid Calls for Government Action

French authorities reported that over 3,000 shops across the country were damaged or looted during last weekend’s protests, with about 450 businesses in Paris specifically affected. The unrest, which began with student-led demonstrations over school conditions and living costs, spread to include broader anti-government sentiment. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched, though union organizers estimated the number to be higher. The protests turned violent in some areas, with shops smashed, museums closed, and police using tear gas and water cannons to control crowds. The French Interior Minister, Laurent Nuñez, announced plans to deploy 70,000 officers and other security measures to prevent further unrest. Meanwhile, a bakery owner, Jhemima Sheilha, described how her shop was destroyed by looters, while influencer Lola-Fleur Whittaker mocked shopkeepers on a television program. The protests have also drawn international attention, with U.S. billionaire Ken Griffin warning that the chaos in France serves as a warning for American youth about the dangers of socialist policies.

Where the accounts differ

The Free Press reports that about 450 businesses in Paris were damaged, with half looted, while CBS News states that 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted. The Free Press attributes the destruction of Sheilha’s bakery to looters, while FOX News mentions that nearly 1,000 people were arrested during the protests. The Guardian and BBC describe the protests as largely peaceful at first, with violence emerging at the end, while The Free Press and CBS News focus more on the destruction and looting. The Guardian and BBC also note that the government estimated 400,000 participants, while CBS News reports union organizers estimated 800,000.

Sources The Free Press · CBS News · Fox Business · FOX News · The Guardian · BBC

Ukraine's Starlink service restored after speed restrictions disrupted military operations

Ukraine's Ministry of Defense announced on Saturday that full access to Starlink and Starshield satellite services has been restored, with stable connectivity at speeds exceeding 250 mph. The restoration followed a week of restrictions that limited the Ukrainian military's ability to use drones for intercepting Russian attack drones and for logistics. President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that the service was restored overnight, improving front-line operations and defense against Russian drones. Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, admitted that his company had throttled Starlink speeds, citing Ukraine's use of the service for offensive drone strikes against people as a violation of terms of service. Musk maintained that the U.S. government controlled Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink used for Ukraine's drone operations and communications.

The restrictions on Starlink and Starshield were at the center of tensions between Ukraine and the Trump administration. Ukrainian officials accused both President Trump and Musk of being responsible for the slowdown, while Trump and Musk denied involvement. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had called Musk to address the issue, contradicting Musk's claim that the U.S. government controlled Starshield. The Ukrainian military reported that the restrictions affected drones traveling at speeds of 100 mph or higher, limiting their operational effectiveness.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that Musk admitted to throttling Starlink speeds and that Zelensky stated the service was restored to pre-restriction levels. Axios states that the Ukrainian defense ministry confirmed the restoration of speeds exceeding 400 km/h, attributing the lifting of restrictions to "direct dialogue" and Zelensky's diplomatic efforts. FOX News claims that a source familiar with the situation said Ukraine received no advance warning of the restrictions, while The Hill notes that the Wall Street Journal contradicted Musk's account, stating that Musk was behind the restrictions. CBS News and Fox Business both mention that Trump denied involvement, while Axios and The Hill note that Trump and Musk denied responsibility, with Axios adding that Trump claimed he would speak to Musk if the service was still restricted.

Sources BBC · CBS News · Axios · The Hill · FOX News · Fox Business

Seven killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, Jordan, killing at least seven people and injuring 40 others. The attack occurred on Friday, according to multiple outlets. Witnesses described scenes of panic as people tried to seek cover during the shooting. Jordan’s health minister confirmed 40 people were injured, while the prime minister condemned the attack as a result of "terrorist ideology and blind extremism." King Abdullah II vowed to retaliate "with an iron fist" against those responsible. Security forces are searching for the attackers, and the incident has prompted increased security measures across Jordan.

The attack took place at St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, in Karak governorate. Footage from Jordanian state television showed three attackers, two with handguns and one with a semiautomatic rifle, approaching the church and firing. Security camera footage verified by Reuters showed the attackers running toward the church’s entrance. Witnesses reported the gunfire lasted several minutes, with some describing the attackers as hiding behind trees and a low wall before fleeing. The attack has been described as a rare incident in Jordan, which is generally stable and has seen previous foiled attacks by Islamist militants.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that the attack resulted in seven deaths, while the BBC initially reported seven killed but later revised the toll to seven. The Guardian and NPR state that 40 people were injured, while the Daily Wire and Just The News report 40 injured. The BBC and The Daily Wire mention that the attack lasted several minutes, while the Guardian and NPR describe the duration as 15 minutes. The Guardian and The Daily Wire attribute the claim about the number of injured to Jordan’s health minister, while the BBC and NPR do not specify the source of that number. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that one of the attackers had a weapon jam, while the BBC and NPR do not. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that the attackers fled in a pickup truck, while the BBC and NPR do not specify the method of escape.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · FOX News · The Daily Wire · NPR · Just The News

Trump advisers still see opportunity for US agenda even if Netanyahu loses: report

President Trump’s advisers reportedly believe a loss by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s election could make it easier to advance the president’s Middle East agenda. US officials told Axios that potential successors to Netanyahu would have strong incentives to maintain close ties with Washington. The potential for progress for Trump’s Middle East agenda in a new political environment comes despite the president’s decision to endorse Netanyahu last Sunday, while Netanyahu trails in the polls against former Israeli Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot. US intelligence is warning Iran is increasing its threats against Americans in the region, with US warships including two aircraft carrier strike groups in the region preparing for a potential escalation. Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot is favored in Tuesday’s elections.

The Guardian reports that Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, is the lead opposition challenger in Tuesday’s Israeli election. Eisenkot has called for a “country without lies” and has spoken positively about Trump’s efforts in the region. The Guardian highlights that Netanyahu has dominated Israeli politics for 19 of the past 30 years, with the election pitting him against a bloc of anti-Netanyahu figures, including former PM Naftali Bennett and Moldova-born Avigdor Lieberman.

The Nation notes that the Israeli election is exposing the façade of Israeli democracy, with the Supreme Court disqualifying a Palestinian candidate for an article describing Hamas’s attack on Israel as a “significant historical event.” The Nation also highlights that every Jewish party in the Knesset supported the disqualification of the Palestinian candidate, showing the fealty of Israel’s so-called opposition to policies of Jewish supremacy.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Guardian differ on the political dynamics of the election. The New York Post states that US officials believe potential successors to Netanyahu would have strong incentives to maintain close ties with Washington, while The Guardian notes that Netanyahu has dominated Israeli politics for 19 of the past 30 years, with the election pitting him against a bloc of anti-Netanyahu figures. The Nation and Al Jazeera differ on the role of Palestinian candidates in the election, with The Nation reporting that the Supreme Court disqualified a Palestinian candidate for an article describing Hamas’s attack on Israel as a “significant historical event,” while Al Jazeera focuses on the online campaign tactics between Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s opposition.

Sources New York Post · The Guardian · The Nation · Al Jazeera · Christian Science Monitor · NPR

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Neil Bush backs Democrat in Texas Senate race, citing concerns over Ken Paxton's record

Neil Bush, a member of the Bush family, has publicly endorsed Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, stating his vote was motivated by concerns over Ken Paxton's record and admiration for Talarico's character. Bush expressed worries about the political culture under Donald Trump, where loyalty to individuals may overshadow loyalty to principles. Talarico is running against Paxton, a Republican and Trump ally, in a closely contested race. The race has drawn significant outside spending, with groups like Lone Star Rising PAC supporting Talarico and the Senate Leadership Fund backing Paxton, which received substantial funding from Elon Musk.

Talarico has faced allegations of sexual misconduct, which were debunked after it was revealed the accuser was not the real person in the video. The incident is linked to Russian disinformation efforts, as similar tactics were used against other Democratic candidates. Talarico has also faced legal challenges, including a lawsuit over the use of the "Change My Mind" slogan, which he claims was trademarked by conservative commentator Steven Crowder.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Neil Bush's support for Talarico is part of a broader family trend, with Barbara Bush also contributing to Talarico's campaign. The Washington Examiner focuses on Latino voter sentiment and the tight race between Paxton and Talarico. The Guardian highlights Talarico's criticism of Elon Musk and his claims about Musk's influence in the race. Mother Jones details the Russian disinformation campaign targeting Talarico, linking it to past efforts against other Democrats. The Federalist discusses the legal battle over the "Change My Mind" slogan and Talarico's attempt to appeal to conservative voters. Newsweek covers the religious aspects of the race, including Paxton's emphasis on faith and Talarico's coalition of religious voters.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · Mother Jones · The Federalist · Newsweek

Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday to elect their next president

Brazilians will vote for their next president on Sunday after neither the incumbent left-wing candidate, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, nor his right-wing opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, garnered a majority of the votes in the election’s first round earlier this month. Bolsonaro, who has the support of President Donald Trump, is the slight favorite heading into Sunday’s runoff, with him leading by roughly one percentage point in the most recent polls released on Saturday, according to Reuters. The two candidates finalized the arguments of their campaigns on Saturday, as Lula marched along Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beach, while Bolsonaro campaigned in a key battleground state.

More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flavio Bolsonaro. Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%. On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports that Bolsonaro leads by one percentage point in the most recent polls, while Newsweek states that the candidates are tied at 50 percent of valid votes. The Guardian mentions that Bolsonaro won the first round with 47% to Lula's 45%, and the Christian Science Monitor notes that Lula earned 3.3 million fewer votes in this year’s first-round election than he did in the 2022 vote. The FOX News account does not mention poll numbers or the first-round results, focusing instead on the voting system and security.

Sources Washington Examiner · Newsweek · The Guardian · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · FOX News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Eleven sustain gunshot wounds in shooting near Florida university

A shooting near a Florida university campus in Tallahassee left 11 people with gunshot wounds and another person injured, authorities reported. The incident occurred near the Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University (FAMU) campus on Perry Street on Saturday night. Police stated that a physical altercation preceded the shooting, though details were not provided. The youngest victim was 11 years old, according to the New York Post. The university emphasized the safety of its students, faculty, and staff, while urging people to avoid the area for the investigation.

Authorities confirmed that the shooting took place near FAMU's Bragg Memorial Stadium, close to the intersection of Perry and Manatee streets. The Tallahassee Police Department reported that 12 people were injured, including 11 with gunshot wounds, with one in critical condition, two seriously injured, and eight in stable condition. The university noted that the incident occurred during its Homecoming Week, and the campus remained safe, though individuals were advised to avoid the area.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Newsweek both report 11 injured, while FOX News, ABC News, CBS News, and the New York Post state 12 injured. The Guardian and Newsweek mention 11 people with gunshot wounds and one other injured, while FOX News, ABC News, CBS News, and the New York Post specify 11 with gunshot wounds and one additional injured person. The New York Post and FOX News include a 12th injured person, a grandmother, who was hurt while fleeing the scene, which is not mentioned in the Guardian or Newsweek. The Guardian and Newsweek do not mention the grandmother's injury. The New York Post and FOX News attribute the youngest victim's age to police, while the Guardian and Newsweek do not specify the youngest victim's age. The Guardian and Newsweek do not mention the football game context, while FOX News, ABC News, CBS News, and the New York Post include it.

Sources The Guardian · FOX News · Newsweek · ABC News · CBS News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels

NPR reports that drinking water in Taiz has reached crisis levels as Houthi rebels besiege the city, with over a million residents struggling to meet basic needs. Families are rationing water, with some paying up to 75% more for bottled water. The siege has also led to shortages of groceries and fuel, impacting hospitals and sanitation. Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to open roads into the city to prevent a humanitarian disaster.

Al Jazeera highlights the dire situation in Taiz's Republican Hospital, where dialysis treatments are being cut back due to shortages of medical supplies and fuel. Doctors warn that the hospital could shut down completely within days. The hospital relies on diesel generators for power, and fuel shortages have forced them to buy diesel on the black market at five times the pre-siege price. The hospital has suspended operations in some departments, and officials warn of a potential complete collapse of healthcare services.

Where the accounts differ

NPR does not mention the specific situation at Taiz's Republican Hospital or the impact on dialysis treatments, while Al Jazeera details the hospital's struggles with fuel and medical supplies. NPR states that the siege began in recent weeks, while Al Jazeera notes that Taiz was previously under Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016. NPR mentions that the city is a strategic gateway to southern Yemen, a detail absent in Al Jazeera's account. Al Jazeera reports that the latest delivery of dialysis solutions was due earlier this month but failed to arrive due to the siege, a detail not included in NPR's coverage.

James Talarico’s Campaign Is a Messaging Machine. I Watched How It Runs.

James Talarico, a state representative running for Senate in Texas, staged a rally at a youth football field in San Marcos, Texas, on a Thursday night. The event was designed to be filmed as part of his campaign strategy, with cameras and a controlled crowd. Talarico, who previously won a state house seat in 2018 by a narrow margin, is now running against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. His campaign is noted for its structured messaging and polished delivery, contrasting with the more spontaneous approach of past Democratic candidates like Beto O’Rourke. Talarico’s team has focused on refining his arguments and delivering them with precision, which has contributed to his strong polling numbers and record fundraising.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that Talarico’s campaign is a “messaging machine” with a focus on efficiency and polished delivery, while The Daily Wire highlights Talarico’s religious background as part of a broader discussion on the role of faith in politics. The Daily Wire does not mention Talarico’s campaign strategy or fundraising, instead focusing on the religious dimensions of various candidates. The Federalist and The Dispatch do not cover Talarico’s campaign at all, with The Dispatch focusing on unrelated topics and The Federalist discussing polling scandals.

Sources Mother Jones · Fox Business · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · The Dispatch

California Redistricting and Ohio Gubernatorial Race Highlight Political Controversies

In California, Republican Jim Desmond is running against Democrat Marni von Wilpert in the 48th Congressional District, which was redrawn in 2025 to shift from a Republican-leaning to a Democratic-leaning district. A poll commissioned by Desmond’s campaign shows von Wilpert leading Desmond 47% to 44% among likely voters. The Cook Political Report rates the race as “Lean Democratic,” with a D+2 partisan voting index. The race has attracted over $6 million in outside spending, with most supporting von Wilpert. Desmond’s campaign claims over $7.5 million has been spent attacking him since September. The Tarrance Group poll also found Newsom unpopular among unaffiliated voters, with 37% viewing him favorably and 53% unfavorably.

In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign released an ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing Acton of lying about her childhood. The ad has sparked controversy, with some Republicans criticizing it as deeply troubling. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, responded by explaining the family’s history of abuse and the estrangement from their mother. The ad has also drawn criticism from political analysts and figures like former GOP candidate Nikki Haley and conservative pundit Meghan McCain. Despite the backlash, Ramaswamy’s campaign confirmed it was behind the ad and plans to spend $4 million promoting it.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Nation both report that Ramaswamy’s ad features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing Acton of lying about her past, but only The Nation and Al Jazeera mention that the ad omits the fact that Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody in 1978 after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The Daily Wire and The Hill describe the ad as part of a broader controversy, but only The Nation and Al Jazeera provide details about the family’s history of abuse and the estrangement. The Daily Wire and The Guardian report on the California redistricting race, while The Hill, The Nation, and Al Jazeera focus on the Ohio gubernatorial race. The Guardian and The Nation provide more context on Vance’s potential presidential ambitions, which are not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Hill · The Guardian · Slate · The Nation · Al Jazeera

Trump Admin Seeks to Block Alaska Senate Result if Dan Sullivan Loses

The Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a lawsuit against the state of Alaska on Thursday, seeking to block the certification of the Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. The lawsuit argues that the presence of another candidate named Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, could have misled voters in Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system. The DOJ claims that the votes for the "decoy" Sullivan could have changed the outcome of the election if they had been cast for the incumbent. The administration has said it aims to stop Alaska from certifying the result if Sullivan loses, amid concerns about voter confusion.

President Donald Trump has publicly supported the DOJ’s legal action, calling the presence of the second Sullivan a "scam" and accusing Democrats of planting the candidate to confuse voters. Trump has repeatedly claimed that even a small number of votes could determine the outcome of the race, which is currently considered one of the closest Senate contests of the year. The DOJ spokesperson stated that the lawsuit is based on the National Voter Registration Act and aims to ensure the integrity of Alaska’s election.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and Mother Jones both report that the DOJ claims the second Sullivan intended to mislead voters, while Al Jazeera and Axios describe the lawsuit as alleging voter confusion without explicitly stating the intent of the second Sullivan. The Hill and Axios note that the DOJ is seeking to delay certification if the incumbent loses, while The Hill also reports that Peltola called the lawsuit a "desperate attempt" to "cling to power." FOX News does not mention the specific Alaska lawsuit but discusses the DOJ’s broader role in election integrity, including a separate case in California.

Sources Newsweek · The Hill · FOX News · Mother Jones · Al Jazeera · Axios

Former FBI Officials Charged With Lying About Hunter Biden Case

Two former FBI officials were charged Friday with lying to Congress about their involvement in the bureau’s investigation into Hunter Biden. The Justice Department said Nikki Cole Floris of Alexandria, Virginia, and Bradley Benavides of Aiken, South Carolina, turned themselves in to federal authorities after both were charged with making false statements. FBI Director Kash Patel stated that the pair allegedly lied about their role in the FBI’s investigations into Hunter Biden, which were part of the now-defunct Foreign Influence Task Force. The charges were filed as part of an ongoing investigation into the task force’s activities. Both defendants were charged with making false statements in a matter within the jurisdiction of the legislative branch. Prosecutors said the pair lied to Congress about their knowledge of the Hunter Biden probe based on documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts.

The FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force, which was dissolved, was tasked with combating foreign influence in the 2020 election. Floris once made headlines after claiming she was “running a shadow government” during her role at the task force. Lawyers for Floris disputed the charges, calling them politically motivated. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said the charges showed that no one is above the law, emphasizing that lying to Congress strikes at the heart of the democratic system.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and New York Post both state that Floris and Benavides denied involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation during congressional interviews, but the New York Post adds that they allegedly helped shape the public narrative about the laptop and provided false information to lawmakers. The New York Post also mentions that Benavides claimed to have learned about the laptop from Wikipedia, while the Daily Wire notes that the Justice Department said this was despite evidence showing their involvement. The Just The News and NPR both mention that the charges are politically motivated and that the timing is close to an election, but the Just The News adds that Republicans see this as the first instance of accountability for the Trump administration’s review of alleged government weaponization. The ABC News and CBS News both note that the charges were filed just before the midterm elections, but CBS News adds that the decision to charge the pair in a criminal complaint is unusual and raises questions about the timing.

Sources The Daily Wire · New York Post · Just The News · NPR · ABC News · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

DNI warned Rubio of 'advanced' Iranian efforts to target US personnel, memo shows

A declassified intelligence memo obtained by multiple outlets warns that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target U.S. personnel abroad, with lethal plotting efforts reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries. The memo, sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, was first reported by Axios. The warning comes days after the State Department ordered the departure of nonessential U.S. personnel from Saudi Arabia due to escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The memo does not mention the evacuation order, though it highlights the heightened threat to U.S. officials.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian infrastructure such as airports and oil facilities. These attacks have led to civilian casualties and prompted Saudi officials to report that their military prevented an attack on the holy city of Medina. The conflict between the Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government has drawn in U.S. military operations, which have been cited as a factor in the escalation of attacks against U.S. interests in the region.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and FOX News both report that the memo was sent to Rubio by Clayton and that it warns of advanced Iranian efforts to target U.S. personnel. However, The Hill notes that the memo does not mention the State Department’s evacuation of personnel from Saudi Arabia, while FOX News states that the memo was first reported by Axios. The Guardian and Al Jazeera do not mention the memo at all, focusing instead on oil prices and attacks on tankers. The Daily Caller and Axios both report the memo’s existence and its contents, with Axios noting that the memo does not identify specific targets or countries outside the Middle East.

Sources The Hill · Al Jazeera · The Daily Caller · FOX News · Axios · The Guardian

Netanyahu’s threat to invade West Bank would test America’s dwindling patience for Israeli conflict

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans for a large-scale military operation in the West Bank following the killing of two Israeli soldiers in a gunfight near Hebron. The attack, which occurred at a temporary checkpoint, involved two Palestinian gunmen armed with an assault rifle and a handgun. According to the Israeli military, the attackers were killed after a 20-minute firefight. Netanyahu described the operation as the largest in the West Bank since 1967 and pledged mass demolitions, forced displacement, and expanded settlements. The operation includes a full lockdown of the West Bank, with Israeli forces conducting raids in multiple areas, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas, and Qalqilya.

Netanyahu’s announcement has drawn criticism from Israeli legal experts and human rights groups, who argue that the tactics resemble collective punishment and could constitute war crimes. The high court issued a temporary order to halt demolitions, citing violations of international law. Israeli officials, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Defense Minister Israel Katz, have explicitly compared the operation to past actions in Gaza and Jenin refugee camps, where thousands were displaced.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both report that Netanyahu announced plans for a large-scale invasion of the West Bank, but the Examiner emphasizes the potential impact on U.S.-Israel relations, while FOX News focuses on the immediate military response. The Guardian and Al Jazeera provide more detailed accounts of the operation, including the involvement of bulldozers, mass demolitions, and the high court’s intervention. The Guardian notes that the attack was attributed to two men with Israeli license plates, while FOX News identifies the attackers as Palestinians from Hebron. The Guardian and BBC mention the involvement of the Israeli military in the attack, while the Examiner and FOX News do not specify the attackers’ nationalities. The Guardian and Al Jazeera report that the operation includes a full lockdown of the West Bank, while the Examiner and FOX News do not mention this detail.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · Straight Arrow News · BBC · FOX News

Violent Protests Disrupt Paris Ahead of NFL Game, Steelers Fan Event Canceled

The Pittsburgh Steelers have canceled a fan event in Paris following violent protests that have swept across the city and other parts of France. The event, planned for a bar in the Bastille neighborhood, was called off due to safety concerns, according to a statement shared with fans. The NFL game between the Steelers and New Orleans Saints is still scheduled for Sunday at the Stade de France. The U.S. State Department has issued a security alert advising Americans in France to "exercise caution" and avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest. The protests, which began as student-led demonstrations over education issues, have escalated into widespread unrest, including looting, property destruction, and clashes with police.

French authorities have imposed curfews in parts of Paris and banned protests in Marseille and Lyon. President Emmanuel Macron has blamed "illegitimate" protests and "seditious acts by ultra-left groups" for the violence, vowing to crack down on such activities. Meanwhile, the NFL has confirmed that preparations for the game continue, with the league working closely with local authorities on security measures.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that the Steelers canceled the fan event due to "recent events in the Bastille neighborhood" and describes the protests as stemming from student dissatisfaction with the education system. Fox Business attributes the unrest to "socialist policies" and cites Ken Griffin's comments about the riots in France and Chicago. Newsweek provides more detail on the U.S. State Department's security alert and mentions the number of arrests and injuries during the protests. Al Jazeera focuses on Macron's planned meeting with student groups and the demands of high school students. FOX News highlights the impact on businesses, including Michele Teboul's family stores being looted, and includes quotes from a business owner. CBS News reports on the scale of police deployment and the closure of major museums in Paris.

Sources The Daily Wire · Fox Business · Newsweek · Al Jazeera · FOX News · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Brazil’s Workers’ Party Is Not Stopping

In the wake of Brazil’s first round of presidential elections on October 4, 2026, left-wing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party (PT) faced a narrow defeat by far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. With neither candidate securing over 50% of the vote, a runoff election is set for October 25. Lula’s campaign has accused Meta of manipulating election content, leading to protests outside the company’s São Paulo office. Meanwhile, Bolsonaro’s party, the Partido Liberal, gained a legislative majority, raising concerns about the consolidation of far-right power in Brazil. Lula’s supporters are mobilizing to secure his re-election, while legal experts warn of potential constitutional changes by Bolsonaro’s camp.

The race has intensified with both candidates vying for a decisive edge in the final days before the runoff. Lula, who previously served as president from 2003 to 2010 and again in 2022, is running for his fourth nonconsecutive term. Bolsonaro, who finished ahead of Lula in the first round, has proposed constitutional reforms that could limit presidential terms and reshape the judiciary. The election has also drawn international attention, with U.S. President Donald Trump remaining largely silent on the race despite his historical support for Bolsonaro.

Where the accounts differ

The Nation and FOX News differ on the role of Meta in the election. The Nation states that Lula’s campaign accused Meta of meddling with the 2026 elections through disinformation campaigns and suppression of left-wing content, leading to protests outside Meta’s São Paulo office. FOX News, however, does not mention Meta’s involvement in the election, instead focusing on Brazil’s electronic voting system and its security. The Nation also notes that Meta announced compliance with an order from the electoral court to provide equal treatment to both candidates, a detail absent in FOX News.

Sources The Nation · NPR · BBC · Newsweek · Christian Science Monitor · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Missile strikes in Kyiv endanger civilians, escalating humanitarian crisis and risking further escalation in the war.

Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine

Russia launched missile strikes on Kyiv shortly after agreeing to resume peace talks with Ukraine. The attacks killed at least two people and injured 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings, and a clinic. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that three missiles carried cluster warheads, one of which struck the Pecherskyi district, damaging historic structures. Zelenskyy accused Russia of not being serious about peace, noting the strikes occurred almost immediately after talks. US envoy Steve Witkoff praised Putin during negotiations, calling him a humanitarian. Zelenskyy responded on social media, sarcastically referring to Russian "humanitarians" launching missiles. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, warned that flattery would not stop Russian aggression. The UK government disputed Witkoff’s description of Putin, noting his role in killing thousands of Ukrainians and his own soldiers.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC both report that Russia launched missile strikes on Kyiv shortly after agreeing to resume peace talks. The Guardian provides more detail on the number of casualties, specific targets, and Zelenskyy’s comments. The BBC mentions the destroyed retail park but does not specify casualties or targets. The Daily Wire does not mention the missile strikes or the peace talks, instead focusing on alleged war crimes and human rights abuses by Russia. The Guardian and BBC both attribute the claim about Witkoff calling Putin a humanitarian to the same source, while the Daily Wire does not mention the peace talks or the missile strikes at all.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · The Daily Wire

Ramaswamy controversy pits Trump, Vance against Ohio GOP establishment

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, faced backlash for an ad featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who criticized Acton’s past. The ad, which claims Acton lied about her history, has drawn criticism from some Ohio Republicans, including Gov. Mike DeWine and Sen. Jon Husted. Acton’s brother stated that the family was estranged from their mother due to her past relationship with the man who allegedly sexually abused Acton as a child. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended Ramaswamy, with Trump calling DeWine a “RINO” and urging Ramaswamy to continue the ad. Meanwhile, other Ohio Republicans, including former Gov. John Kasich and former Sen. Rob Portman, have criticized the ad as crossing the line. The controversy has also put Husted in an awkward position, as he faces a tough race against Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and Just The News both mention Trump calling DeWine a “RINO,” but The Hill adds that Trump said Ramaswamy “should keep it up” in a Truth Social post, while Just The News attributes this statement to Trump directly. The Hill and Washington Examiner both note that Husted said he “would not have run” the ad, but The Hill adds that Husted’s statement was made to the Associated Press, while Washington Examiner attributes it to the same source. The Hill and Just The News both describe the ad as featuring Acton’s mother insinuating she has mental health issues, but Just The News adds that the ad claims Acton “lies about her past” and “needs help.” The Hill and Washington Examiner both mention Acton’s brother’s statement about the family estrangement, but The Hill adds that the estrangement began when Acton was 12, while Washington Examiner does not specify the age.

Sources The Hill · Mother Jones · Washington Examiner · Newsweek · Just The News · FOX News

Mike Rogers Used His Last Debate to Smear Abdul El-Sayed

Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed in their final debate, focusing on rising costs, the war in Iran, and ICE policies. El-Sayed accused Rogers of supporting the Trump administration’s war in Iran, which he claimed has raised gas and grocery prices. Rogers responded by accusing El-Sayed of being a "sock puppet" for Trump and questioned his loyalty to the Constitution. The debate also featured accusations from Rogers about El-Sayed’s alleged ties to terrorist groups, which El-Sayed denied. Rogers also distanced himself from some of Trump’s policies, including the Canadian tariffs, while El-Sayed continued to tie Rogers to Trump’s agenda.

Rogers and El-Sayed exchanged accusations throughout the debate, with Rogers suggesting El-Sayed was trying to avoid past positions and was influenced by foreign groups. El-Sayed countered by calling Rogers’ claims "shameful" and emphasizing his commitment to the Constitution. The debate highlighted the candidates’ differing views on foreign policy, economic issues, and national security, with both candidates attempting to frame the other as untrustworthy.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Hill both report that Rogers accused El-Sayed of being influenced by the Muslim Brotherhood and having donors from Hamas and Hezbollah. CBS News and The Daily Wire also mention these claims, but FOX News and Washington Examiner do not specify which groups El-Sayed is allegedly connected to. The Daily Wire adds that Rogers accused El-Sayed of deleting social media posts related to his past positions on policing, a detail not included in other accounts. Mother Jones and CBS News both mention that El-Sayed’s half-sister posted about his mother’s alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, while The Hill and The Daily Wire reference this as well. FOX News does not mention the social media posts or the half-sister’s claims.

Sources Mother Jones · CBS News · The Hill · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire

Ilhan Omar says US agents seized 17 items in raid designed to ‘freak’ her out

Federal agents raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on October 12, 2026, as part of an immigration fraud investigation. Omar described the search as intrusive but polite, noting that agents took 17 items, including phones, notebooks, and a Somali language children’s book. She claimed the raid was intended to intimidate her, with agents arriving early in the morning and conducting a thorough search of her home. Omar denied allegations of immigration fraud, stating she is confident she did nothing wrong. The raid has raised concerns about the timing, with some lawmakers questioning whether the investigation was politically motivated, especially given the proximity to the November midterms.

Omar, who was born in Somalia and became a U.S. citizen in 2000, has been a frequent target of President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly criticized her character and background. During a Wednesday interview with MS Now, Omar expressed her intention to move out of her D.C. home due to threats she has received. She also criticized Trump for his attacks, calling him a “sick, very dishonest person who hates our country.”

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and ABC News both report that Omar was taken to the raid by agents who arrived at 6 a.m. and seized 17 items, including phones and notebooks. The Hill and Washington Examiner also mention the same details, though The Hill adds that Omar’s husband’s gift, a vintage camera, was among the items taken. FOX News states that Omar’s passport and phone were seized, but does not specify the number of items taken. The New York Post mentions that Omar’s husband’s notebooks and a Somali phrase book were among the items taken, but does not mention the total number of items. The Guardian and ABC News both attribute the claim that the raid was intended to “freak” Omar out to her, while FOX News attributes a similar sentiment to her in a different context.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · The Hill · Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post

Feds Arrest Powerful Virginia Democrat In Cannabis Corruption Probe

Federal agents arrested Virginia Democrat powerbroker Louise Lucas in a “large-scale” racketeering and money laundering conspiracy tied to a cannabis business she co-owns. Lucas, a state senator and one of the most powerful figures in Virginia’s Democratic Party, surrendered to authorities Thursday, according to the Justice Department. The 82-year-old was indicted on five counts: racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to launder money, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, and maintaining a drug-involved premises. Six others, including Lucas’ daughters and grandson, were also charged and arrested in connection with the alleged scheme.

The indictment, unsealed on Thursday, charges Lucas and six other defendants, including several of her relatives, with drug trafficking, money laundering, and bribery. Federal prosecutors allege that Lucas led a multi-year scheme to enrich her family through a marijuana enterprise, using her position as chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the operation from state law enforcement. The FBI raided Lucas’ office and a cannabis dispensary linked to her in May, and the probe into Lucas, who represents the city of Portsmouth, was launched during former President Joe Biden’s administration.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Guardian both report that Lucas was indicted on five counts, while The Daily Caller and CBS News state she faces five of eight charges. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the claim about Lucas accumulating nearly $5 million in ill-gotten gains to FBI Director Kash Patel, while The Daily Caller and CBS News attribute it to a law enforcement source. The Guardian and CBS News mention that Lucas was charged with conspiracy to commit money laundering, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not specify the exact charges beyond the indictment. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that Lucas was charged with maintaining a drug-involved premises, which is not mentioned in The Daily Caller or CBS News. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the quote about “I’ve gotten too old to not be greedy” to a February 2026 conversation with an unindicted co-conspirator, while The Daily Caller and CBS News do not attribute the quote to a specific source.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Guardian · FOX News · Straight Arrow News · CBS News

Wedgewood Polls Admits to Fabricating Data in Polling Scandal

Wedgewood Polls, a polling firm that had its data cited by major media outlets and polling aggregators, admitted to fabricating survey results in a statement released on social media. The firm claimed the project was a "social experiment" designed to expose vulnerabilities in the polling industry. The New York Times and Decision Desk HQ both stated they removed Wedgewood's polls from their databases after the admission. The firm's data was included in several major outlets, including The Washington Examiner, The Guardian, and The New York Times.

The scandal has raised concerns about the integrity of polling data and how it is vetted by media and aggregators. Some candidates, like Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow, claimed that Wedgewood's polls influenced their campaign strategies, leading to a drop in donations and volunteer morale. The firm's data was also cited in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, where socialist Francesca Hong was shown as having an edge over Republican candidate Tom Tiffany.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner states that the operation was run by career pollsters from both sides of the political aisle, while The Guardian and The New York Post report that Wedgewood was founded by college students with scant professional experience. The Daily Wire and The New York Post mention that Wedgewood claimed to have two members, one progressive and one conservative, while The Guardian and Straight Arrow News note that the firm's website listed no employee names, phone number, or location. The Daily Wire and The New York Post also report that Wedgewood admitted to fabricating data and claimed it was an experiment, while The Guardian and The Washington Examiner describe the firm as a "shady outfit" and a "fraudulent polling firm."

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · New York Post · Straight Arrow News · FOX News

Biden-Appointed Judge Blocks DHS Noncitizen Voting Investigations in Nine States

A federal judge appointed by former President Joe Biden issued a preliminary injunction Wednesday, halting the Trump administration’s investigation into suspected noncitizen voting in nine states. The order, issued by U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, restricts DHS from conducting field operations targeting individuals who are known, suspected, or reasonably should be suspected of being U.S. citizens. The ruling applies to California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin, and remains in effect until Election Day on Nov. 3. The judge paused her order until 5 p.m. Friday to allow the administration time to appeal.

Martínez-Olguín ruled that the methods used by DHS to identify potential noncitizen voters, including state voter rolls, commercial databases, and AI tools, were unreliable and could lead to the wrongful identification of U.S. citizens. She found that the initiative likely violated a federal law prohibiting the intimidation of individuals who assist or encourage others to vote. The plaintiffs in the case include the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United, the Voto Latino Foundation, and local governments in San Francisco and Santa Clara County.

The Department of Homeland Security defended its methods, stating that agents use multiple sources to verify identities and eliminate false positives. A spokesperson said the agency is focused on identifying and removing noncitizens who vote, while noting it has no plans to investigate individuals believed to be U.S. citizens.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and FOX News both mention that the judge was born in Mexico and nominated by Biden, while The Guardian and CBS News refer to her as a Mexican-born judge. The Daily Wire and CBS News note that the judge worked for the American Civil Liberties Union, while FOX News explicitly states she worked for the ACLU. The Guardian and CBS News describe the judge as having worked for the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project and the National Immigration Law Center, while The Daily Wire and FOX News attribute her prior work to the ACLU. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the judge’s confirmation by the Senate in February 2023, while FOX News does not specify the confirmation date. The Guardian and CBS News state that the judge’s ruling was based on the unreliability of the data used by DHS, while FOX News adds that the judge found the methods could constitute intimidation due to the use of armed agents.

Sources The Daily Wire · NPR · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Department of Justice opens criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has launched a criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski, a former political adviser to Donald Trump and top aide at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The probe follows a referral from the DHS inspector general, according to multiple sources. Lewandowski, who served as a special government employee under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, is under scrutiny over allegations that he profited from his role in the agency. A lawyer for Lewandowski, Adam Trigg, stated that his client has not been contacted by the DOJ and denies any wrongdoing. The investigation is in its early stages, with no subpoenas or legal demands issued yet.

President Trump expressed support for the investigation, stating he wants his staff to be honest and that dishonesty amounts to stealing from him. He said he would not interfere with any prosecutions of dishonest officials. The DOJ has not yet commented on the matter, though it has previously dismissed cases involving Trump allies.

Where the accounts differ

THE GUARDIAN reports that the investigation began with a criminal referral from the DHS inspector general and that Lewandowski signed some DHS contracts despite questionable legal authority. ABC NEWS states that the probe is examining contracting activities at DHS and that Lewandowski served as a special government employee during Noem's tenure, effectively acting as her chief of staff. FOX NEWS adds that Lewandowski was fired from DHS after Trump ousted Noem in March, citing congressional testimony where Noem claimed Trump approved a $220 million ad campaign. THE DAILY WIRE and THE DAILY CALLER both mention that the inspector general’s investigation initially focused on a $220 million advertising contract featuring Noem and that Lewandowski allegedly sought compensation from GEO Group, a private prison company, which declined the requests. THE NEW YORK POST notes that Lewandowski was swept out of DHS following Trump’s firing of Noem and that allegations of misconduct involving Lewandowski’s role in DHS contracting have been reported for over a year.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

LeBron shrugs off Trump blast in home debut win for Philadelphia 76ers

LeBron James contributed 17 points, 10 rebounds, and five assists as the Philadelphia 76ers completed a 29-point comeback to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 in James’s first home game with the team. The victory came hours after Trump criticized James for appearing to practice basketball and golf shots during the national anthem at a game earlier this season. Tyrese Maxey scored 32 points, and Joel Embiid added 24, including a crucial jump shot with 6:54 left in the game. The win marked the largest comeback in the 76ers’ play-by-play era and the largest comeback of James’s career.

The 76ers overcame a first-half deficit of 22 points, with Maxey and Jaylen Brown leading the charge. The team outscored the Cavaliers 60-37 in the second half, clamping down defensively and limiting turnovers. James, who has not responded to Trump’s criticism, called the win “great” but emphasized the team should not rely on such comebacks. “You don’t want to put yourself in too many of those situations,” he said.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both report that Trump criticized James for appearing to practice basketball and golf shots during the national anthem, but only The Guardian attributes the criticism to Trump’s statement at a campaign rally. The Guardian also notes that James called the criticism “a slow news day at the office,” while Al Jazeera reports that James has not made any public response. The Guardian and Newsweek both mention that Trump called James a “TOTAL DISGRACE,” but only Newsweek attributes this to a post on Truth Social. The Guardian and The Federalist both note that Trump has criticized athletes for their behavior during the national anthem, but only The Guardian and Newsweek provide specific examples of past criticism, including Trump’s comments on Colin Kaepernick.

Sources Al Jazeera · BBC · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · The Guardian · Newsweek

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as AI reshapes workforce, displacing thousands in financial sector.

Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances

Barclays announced plans to cut 5,000 jobs as part of broader cost-saving measures, with executives attributing the cuts to advances in AI and ongoing modernization efforts. The job cuts will represent about 5% of the bank’s global workforce of 93,000, with 1,000 positions already eliminated. The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, stated the cuts are part of plans to save over £1.1bn by 2027. The chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, described AI as the “icing on the cake” to modernizing the bank’s technology, emphasizing that the bulk of efficiency gains come from years of investment in technology and process simplification. Barclays also announced a £500m share buyback, bringing total shareholder distributions since January to £2.8bn.

The bank reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits for the July to September quarter, up 12% from the same period last year. This performance is expected to justify potential increases in bank taxes in the upcoming budget. Venkatakrishnan stated Barclays could absorb higher taxes but emphasized the importance of proportion and market signaling. The bank also noted a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, which has become a focus for campaigners pushing for a bank tax.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Barclays’ job cuts are part of wider cost-saving plans driven by AI, with Venkatakrishnan calling AI the “icing on the cake.” The BBC states that not all cuts are due to AI, and that the bank’s efficiency gains come from years of investment in technology. The Daily Caller notes that AI is not solely responsible for the cuts, with Venkatakrishnan emphasizing the need for infrastructure to realize AI benefits. The Guardian and BBC both mention that 60% of the cuts will affect support functions, including developers, while the Daily Caller attributes this to Reuters, which is not cited in the other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right covered this story.
