Trump Persuades Putin To Free Jailed American Teacher Who Was Taken On Biden’s Watch

President Donald Trump claimed to have persuaded Russian President Vladimir Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American teacher detained in Russia for over four years. Hubbard was released and was waiting at a St. Petersburg airport for his flight back to the U.S. according to U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff. The State Department had previously labeled Hubbard as wrongfully detained. Trump stated that he had made the request to Putin during a phone call last week, and that no prisoner swap was needed. Hubbard was seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022 and was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison in October 2024 for allegedly serving as a mercenary for Ukraine. His family and legal team denied the charges, claiming he was too old to fight and had never owned a gun.

During a meeting in St. Petersburg, Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, calling him a "humanitarian." This prompted backlash from some U.S. lawmakers, including Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who criticized Witkoff's comments. Putin also announced his readiness to resume trilateral peace talks with the U.S. and Ukraine, though these talks have been rejected by Ukraine. The meeting included discussions on a potential framework agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that Trump took a swipe at former President Joe Biden, stating that Hubbard was taken on Biden’s watch and that the previous administration’s talks with the Kremlin went nowhere. This is not mentioned in Axios, NPR, or CBS News. The New York Post and BBC include Witkoff’s praise of Putin as a “humanitarian,” which is not mentioned in The Daily Wire or Axios. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention that Trump claimed to have made the request directly to Putin, while Axios and BBC do not specify the method of communication. The Daily Wire and CBS News state that no prisoner swap was needed, while Axios and BBC do not explicitly state this. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention that Hubbard was in poor health and would be flown to Texas for treatment, while Axios and BBC do not specify his health condition.

Sources The Daily Wire · Axios · NPR · New York Post · BBC · CBS News

Sea mine crisis re-emerges in Strait of Hormuz as Tehran urges Washington to accept deal

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy reported that two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters, citing Iran's official Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA). Both tankers were carrying about 2 million barrels of crude oil. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) warned that sea mines pose a serious threat to vessels navigating the strategic waterway, with IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez stating that the traffic separation scheme, approved in 1968, is still in place but not guaranteed to be clear of mines. The developments came amid stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran over ending the conflict.

The U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks intensified, according to a spokesperson. The order applies only to Saudi Arabia, though reports suggest similar measures may be taken in other Gulf countries. The Houthis have attacked civilian airports and critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, leading to civilian casualties and travel disruptions. The U.S. is also considering military action against the Houthis, with President Trump weighing direct strikes.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the IRGC navy said two tankers caught fire after striking mines, while CBS News states that Iran's IRGC claimed to have hit four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf. CBS also mentions that three other ships caught fire after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz. The Hill and Just The News both report the U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency employees and families to leave Saudi Arabia, but The Hill adds that the U.S. is preparing to issue similar orders for embassies in the UAE, Jordan, Qatar, and Bahrain. New York Post and CBS News both mention Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, with CBS providing specific casualty numbers.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · The Hill · Just The News · The Guardian · CBS News

Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users

A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties after a jury found the company misled users about data privacy. The ruling follows a trial where jurors determined Meta violated New Mexico’s consumer protection laws over 43 million times. The judge reduced the potential penalty from over $219 billion to $25 billion, citing state law. Meta has stated it plans to appeal the decision. The case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the firm harvested data from millions of Facebook users without consent. The state accused Meta of failing to inform users about data access and mishandling harmful content.

The case is part of a broader trend of lawsuits against Meta over data privacy and user safety. In August, the company agreed to pay $17 billion to settle similar claims with 47 states and the District of Columbia. New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, called the ruling a significant victory for consumer protection. Meta argued the penalty is excessive and could deter businesses from operating in the state.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that the judge mentioned Facebook’s content moderation shortcomings and that the case was broadened to criticize the company’s strategy, including its shift from internal fact-checkers to community notes. This detail is not present in the other accounts. The Daily Wire also claims that Torrez criticized Meta for abandoning its fact-check program after Trump’s 2024 election win, a claim not included in the other reports. The Daily Wire attributes the claim about Torrez meeting with other Democrat attorneys general to the outlet itself, while other accounts do not mention this.

Sources Axios · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News · Straight Arrow News · Fox Business

Ilhan Omar vacating DC apartment after federal raid, citing death threats

Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) stated she will be forced to move away from her Washington, D.C., apartment due to death threats she received following a federal investigation. The raid occurred after federal agents executed a search warrant at her residence, seizing 17 items including her phone and other electronics. Omar described the agents as “intrusive but polite,” and noted they logged the items they took and returned the rest. She also mentioned that her children’s safety is a concern, as her address is public and she has received death threats.

Federal authorities are investigating potential immigration fraud in Omar’s family’s paperwork, including allegations that she participated in a sham marriage with her brother to gain U.S. residency. The Justice Department has not provided detailed information about the case, though a court filing indicates that the search warrant for her D.C. home has not been fully executed. Omar denies wrongdoing and claims the investigation is politically motivated, accusing the Trump administration of waging a “campaign of political intimidation” against her.

Omar has received support from Democratic colleagues and former President Obama, who condemned the investigation as “appalling.” She also expressed confidence that she has done nothing wrong, stating she is “a person of enormous faith” and will continue to fight for her beliefs.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Hill both report that Omar received death threats following the federal raid, while The Guardian and The Daily Wire describe the raid as an attempt to “freak” her out and as part of a broader political feud with Trump. The Daily Wire notes that the DOJ has not fully executed the search warrant, while The Guardian and The Hill do not mention this. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also include details about the timing of the raid and its potential political implications, which are not present in the Washington Examiner or ABC News accounts. The FOX News account provides additional information about Omar’s daughters appearing at the scene of the raid and her husband’s public comments, which are not included in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Hill · ABC News · The Guardian · The Daily Wire · FOX News

El-Sayed and Rogers clash in Michigan Senate debate over policy, national security and Trump alignment

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers faced off in their second and final debate for Michigan’s open Senate seat, with El-Sayed repeatedly accusing Rogers of being a "sock puppet" for President Trump. El-Sayed criticized Rogers for aligning with Trump on trade issues, calling the president’s tariffs on Canada "not well thought through." Rogers, in turn, accused El-Sayed of being a "corporate politician" and questioned his loyalty to the United States, linking him to the Muslim Brotherhood and suggesting his donors were tied to Hamas, Hezbollah and the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed denied any such ties, calling the accusations "shameful" and "beneath" Rogers.

The debate also featured sharp exchanges over policy positions, with El-Sayed branding Rogers' platform as a "MAGA vision" and Rogers accusing El-Sayed of a "pattern of deception." El-Sayed called Rogers' attacks on him "MAGA bingo," suggesting the Republican relied on Trump-aligned talking points. Rogers countered by accusing El-Sayed of using Trump as a central focus in his campaign, suggesting the debate should track how often El-Sayed mentioned Trump.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that El-Sayed mentioned Trump 18 times during the debate, while The Hill states that El-Sayed "repeatedly" invoked Trump but does not specify a number. The Daily Wire and CBS News both mention El-Sayed's family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, but CBS News notes that El-Sayed has disavowed any connection to the organization, while The Daily Wire cites internal Brotherhood documents and claims El-Sayed has struggled to answer questions about his ties. The Hill and CBS News both mention that Rogers accused El-Sayed of having donors tied to Hamas, Hezbollah and the Muslim Brotherhood, but CBS News adds that El-Sayed has denied these claims, while The Hill notes that El-Sayed's half-sister posted social media content suggesting his mother supported the Muslim Brotherhood.

Sources FOX News · The Hill · The Daily Wire · CBS News · Washington Examiner · ABC News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Supreme Court Blocks Trump Admin Bid to Restrict Transgender Medical Care for Federal Prisoners

The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration’s request to immediately enforce new restrictions on transgender medical care for federal prisoners. The court’s order did not explain its reasoning, but it noted that conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would have granted the administration’s request to pause a lower court’s order blocking the policy. The Justice Department plans to continue defending the policy before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The policy, which limits medical treatments and social accommodations for transgender prisoners, was introduced under an executive order from President Trump. The policy was supported by an executive order from Trump, though the Bureau of Prisons said it adopted the policy independently, citing security concerns and its determination that standards pushed by the World Professional Association for Transgender Health were not reliable. The policy was challenged by three transgender prisoners, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, who argued it was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, appointed by President Ronald Reagan, blocked the policy after finding that the prisoners were likely to succeed on their claim that it was arbitrary and capricious. The judge also directed the Bureau of Prisons to continue providing medical treatment for the transgender-identifying prisoners under its prior policy.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Guardian differ on the number of transgender prisoners in federal detention, with The Daily Wire stating there are about 1,000 and The Guardian reporting over 2,000. The Federalist and The New York Post mention the Bureau of Prisons adopted the policy independently, while The Guardian and ABC News attribute the policy to the executive order from Trump. The Federalist and The New York Post note that the policy was a successor to a 2025 version, while The Guardian and The Daily Wire do not specify the timeline. The Guardian and The Federalist mention the policy’s extension to “social accommodations,” while The Daily Wire and ABC News describe it as including “social accommodations” but do not specify what they entail.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Federalist · The Guardian · ABC News · New York Post

Trump attacks Democratic challenger Hamilton at Kansas rally as Senate race tightens

President Donald Trump took the stage in ruby-red Kansas on Monday night to campaign for Sen. Roger Marshall, a one-term incumbent facing a surprisingly close race against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. Trump unleashed a series of personal and baseless attacks against Hamilton at the rally in Park City, Kansas, with just two weeks out from election day as the balance of power in the Senate hangs in the balance. He also returned to anti-Muslim and anti-immigration rhetoric, directing criticism at Muslim figures including Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

During the rally, Trump was interrupted by five protesters during four incidents and, after one of the interruptions, he remarked on the “great law enforcement” who swiftly escorted the interrupters out of the rally. Trump’s remarks about the Kansas law enforcement came as news broke not long before that a local man will be facing a federal charge for allegedly threatening to shoot the president ahead of his Wichita rally.

In a separate debate, candidates Roger Marshall and Adam Hamilton clashed over Trump policies, Senate control, and the impact of tariffs, the Iran war, and other Trump administration policies on the state. Marshall argued that Hamilton leans further to the left than he has let on, questioning how independent Hamilton would be. Hamilton described himself as a "moderate or independent-minded Democrat" and vowed to "work across the aisle to try to bring people together to solve problems."

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and called him a target of Trump and Republicans, while CBS News attributes the characterization of El-Sayed as a target to El-Sayed himself. FOX News states that Marshall was questioned about a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills, while The New York Post attributes the same claim to the New York Times. The Hill and CBS News both mention that Hamilton criticized the Biden administration's border policies as a "disaster," while FOX News and ABC News attribute the same claim to Hamilton.

Sources ABC News · CBS News · Axios · The Hill · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Trump cites French protests in warning to Kansas voters: ‘Never happening here’

President Donald Trump warned Kansas voters during a rally for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) that the United States could face similar unrest to France, which he claimed is being “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists.” Trump described the French protests as a cautionary tale, urging Americans to avoid the fate of France. The unrest in France, which began as student-led demonstrations over education and living costs, escalated into widespread riots, looting, and clashes with police, with some cities imposing overnight curfews.

French President Emmanuel Macron attributed the unrest to a combination of economic grievances, including rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which he linked to the war in Iran. Macron also condemned the violence as the work of “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.” The protests, which drew hundreds of thousands of participants, saw some 2,400 arrests in a single day and widespread damage to infrastructure and businesses.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that Trump claimed France is being “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists,” while the New York Post and Newsweek attribute the same claim to Trump. The Axios and The Guardian accounts state that Macron linked the unrest to the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while the FOX News account attributes the same claims to Macron and includes a quote from Lisa Daftari, an Iran expert, who disputes Macron’s explanation. The New York Post and Newsweek also mention that Trump claimed the unrest was about “immigration, not schools,” a claim not present in the Washington Examiner or The Guardian accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post · Axios · The Guardian · Newsweek

Ohio governor’s race takes ugly turn with viral video featuring Acton’s mother

A viral video targeting Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, has sparked controversy in the race against GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy. The clip features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling Acton a “liar” and urging voters to reject her. The video, which has circulated widely on social media, does not include a disclaimer about who paid for it. Acton’s campaign has condemned the ad, calling it a “despicable low” and accusing Ramaswamy of exploiting her personal history. Acton, a former director of the Ohio Department of Health, has spoken publicly about her childhood, including allegations of abuse by her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, who was charged with rape in 1978 but never convicted. The video does not directly reference the abuse allegations but challenges Acton’s account of living in a tent during her youth. Ramaswamy’s campaign has defended the ad, claiming that multiple people who know Acton “have told voters not to vote for her.”

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and CBS News both mention that Donna Arthur’s husband, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping Acton in 1978, but The Hill provides more detail about the court records, including that Cledith Arthur was a fugitive until at least 1981 and that the charges were dropped. The New York Post and CBS News state that Acton’s mother stayed married to Cledith Arthur until his death in 2004, while The Hill notes that Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said their mother remained married to Cledith Arthur until he died. The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire do not mention the court records or the fugitive status of Cledith Arthur. The New York Post and CBS News both include the claim that Acton’s mother stayed married to Cledith Arthur until his death, while The Hill and The Daily Wire do not. The Washington Examiner states that Ramaswamy is investing $4 million in the ad, a claim not made by other outlets.

Sources The Hill · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Daily Wire · NPR · CBS News

U.S. support for Ukraine has significantly decreased under Trump administration

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concerns over the reduced U.S. military and financial support for Ukraine, noting a dramatic shift in policy since President Trump returned to office. Former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, William Taylor, stated that assistance to Ukraine has dropped by 95%, with the U.S. no longer providing weapons, ammunition, or financial support. Zelenskyy has emphasized the importance of international support, particularly from the U.S., in the ongoing conflict. Meanwhile, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) has publicly stated she would prefer to keep sanctions on Russia, arguing that the U.S. should continue applying pressure on Moscow to end the war. The Trump administration has waived sanctions on Russia, including those under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, and has signed an oil deal with Moscow, which has drawn criticism from several Republicans.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that U.S. military support has dropped by 95% and that the U.S. is no longer providing weapons or ammunition to Ukraine. The Hill states that Sen. Darline Graham expressed her preference to keep sanctions on Russia, while ABC News highlights the Trump administration's efforts to secure the release of American citizens detained in Russia, including Stephen Hubbard. Axios and BBC both mention the impact of Trump's energy deals with Russia on the war effort and U.S.-Ukraine relations, with Axios noting the administration's rationale for the diesel deal as a "carrot" to encourage a peace deal. The Free Press adds that the Trump administration may be withholding early warning systems from Ukraine and is aligning with Russia, a claim not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources NPR · The Hill · ABC News · Axios · BBC · The Free Press

Jalen Hurts Diagnosed With Blood Clots in Lungs After Playing in London Game

Jalen Hurts, the Philadelphia Eagles' quarterback, was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli after playing in the team's Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on October 11, 2026. The Eagles initially reported a superficial blood clot in Hurts' calf, which was discovered during an ultrasound in London before the game. Hurts played the game despite being told not to sleep due to the risk of the clot spreading. He later underwent further testing in Philadelphia, which revealed the condition had worsened. Hurts is now on blood thinners and is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season. The Eagles and Hurts' agent stated he is clinically stable and will not return to football activities until he is off medication.

The Eagles' medical staff and coach Nick Sirianni defended their handling of Hurts' condition, emphasizing that the decision to play him was based on the advice of medical experts. Sirianni stated that the team's priority is the health of the players and that the same doctors who helped the team win the Super Bowl were involved in Hurts' care. The team also noted that Hurts was hospitalized in London until 4 a.m. before the game and was advised not to sleep.

Where the accounts differ

The Nation reports that Hurts may have taken a nap at the stadium before the game, though this is unclear, while The Daily Wire states that Hurts did not sleep for 36 hours before the game. The Guardian notes that Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, clarified that he did get some sleep before the game. ABC News and The Daily Caller both mention that Hurts was hospitalized in London until 4 a.m. and that the team's medical staff advised him not to sleep. The Nation and The Guardian attribute the claim about Hurts not sleeping to Tom Pelissero, an NFL insider, who later walked back the “awake for 36 hours” part, which was disputed by Hurts' agent.

Sources The Nation · ABC News · Newsweek · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger

Elon Musk confirmed that Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a potential merger, with both companies forming special committees to assess the possibility. Musk stated that while he supports the idea, the merger is not guaranteed and would require shareholder approval. He emphasized that the committees have not yet reached an agreement on the terms of any potential deal. Musk also highlighted the complementary nature of the companies' work in areas such as artificial intelligence, chip design, and robotics. The merger would create a combined entity with a market value exceeding $3.5 trillion, making it the largest corporate tie-up in history. SpaceX reported its first quarterly profit, and Tesla shares rose following Musk's comments.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster, a car equipped with SpaceX-designed thrusters, was described by some as a symbolic gesture hinting at the potential merger. The vehicle performed a midair maneuver during its recent showcase, though it was noted that it can only briefly elevate rather than fully fly. Musk has also mentioned that the Roadster will be the last manually drivable car Tesla builds, signaling a shift toward autonomous vehicles and robotics.

Where the accounts differ

Slate reports that the Roadster can only "briefly elevate" and that Musk is pushing for a SpaceX-Tesla merger to rescue Tesla's balance sheet. Al Jazeera and Axios state that Musk has formed special committees to explore the merger, but it is not guaranteed. BBC notes that Musk cannot participate in shareholder discussions due to his dual role as CEO of both companies. Fox Business mentions that Musk has pledged to give every child in America a SpaceX share next year, a claim not present in other accounts. Just The News includes a quote from Misty Severi, a reporter, which is absent in other outlets.

Sources Slate · Al Jazeera · Axios · BBC · Just The News · Fox Business

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump’s Voter Raids Have Begun

Federal authorities in California arrested at least 11 people and charged 28 others with alleged voter fraud, including registering as noncitizens and casting ballots. The operation, called “Operation Protect the Vote,” is part of the Trump administration’s efforts to address claims of noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. The Justice Department alleges that all 28 charged individuals are legal permanent residents but not U.S. citizens. The administration has threatened to criminally investigate local officials who process ballots from those on a federal list of suspected noncitizens.

The Justice Department sent California election officials a list of 20,000 people it claims are “likely noncitizens” registered to vote. Officials rejected the demand to withhold ballots, prompting the Justice Department to sue for a court order to prevent California from counting ballots from those on the list. The Trump administration has also threatened local officials with criminal prosecution for processing those ballots.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Federalist both report that the Justice Department charged 28 people, with 11 arrested. The Daily Wire states that 28 foreigners were arrested, with at least 11 in custody. The Dispatch provides no specific numbers or details about arrests or charges. The Federalist mentions that 23 of the 28 charged allegedly voted in U.S. elections, a claim not made by Mother Jones or The Daily Wire. The Daily Wire includes specific cases, such as Alexander Muñoz and Amandeep Kaur, which are not detailed in the other accounts. The Federalist also notes that Leslie Stahl downplayed noncitizen voting on CBS News, a detail absent from the other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · The Daily Wire · The Dispatch · The Federalist

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Trump unveils $25M whistleblower program offering up to $30,000 for fraud tips

President Donald Trump announced a new Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program during an Oval Office event with Vice President JD Vance and independent journalist Nick Shirley. The program offers rewards for tips leading to fraud convictions or significant federal enforcement actions. Trump stated that whistleblowers could receive 1% of the amount of fraud they report, with individual awards capped at $30,000. The White House said the initiative is administered by the Justice Department and that Americans can report suspected fraud through fraud.gov. Trump also mentioned he would personally resolve disputes over reward distribution.

The program was described as a significant expansion of efforts to combat taxpayer fraud, with Trump emphasizing the importance of holding fraudsters accountable. The White House credited independent journalist Nick Shirley with prompting increased federal law enforcement activity in Minnesota, which led to investigations, arrests, and new charges against several individuals and organizations linked to alleged fraud at Somali-run daycare centers.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Trump described a different payout structure, stating journalists could also participate, subject to approval from their employers. It also mentions that a White House official initially described a $25 million initiative with rewards of up to $30,000. The Daily Wire and CBS News both state that the program caps individual awards at $30,000, while FOX News does not mention a cap. The New York Post and CBS News note that Trump said there is no limit to whistleblower compensation, contradicting the cap mentioned by other outlets. The Daily Wire and CBS News also mention that Trump presented a $10,000 check to Nick Shirley, while FOX News and the New York Post do not specify the amount given to Shirley.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · CBS News · New York Post · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Australian MP Helen Haines critically injured in alleged targeted car attack, remains in stable condition

A 43-year-old man, Brendan Nugent, has been charged with causing serious injury to independent MP Helen Haines after she was allegedly rammed twice by a Toyota LandCruiser outside her office in Wangaratta, Victoria. Haines, 65, was airlifted to a Melbourne hospital where she underwent surgery and had both legs amputated. Her husband, Phil Haines, stated she remains stable and is recovering from the injuries. Nugent, who appeared in court without requesting bail, is expected to face further charges. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the incident as a deliberate act, though the motive remains unknown. Police and intelligence agencies are investigating the attack, which has raised concerns about the safety of politicians in Australia.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Al Jazeera both report that Haines lost both legs, while the ABC News and NPR describe her losing both legs as well. The Guardian and Al Jazeera mention that Nugent was charged with causing harm to a Commonwealth public official, while the BBC and NPR do not specify this charge. The Guardian and Al Jazeera attribute the claim about Nugent’s mental health and neurological condition to his lawyer, Chirag Patel, while the ABC News and NPR do not mention this detail. The Guardian and Al Jazeera report that a bystander, Ricky Jefferies, intervened and removed a knife from Nugent, while the BBC and NPR do not mention this specific detail. The Guardian and Al Jazeera state that the AFP and Victoria police had no intelligence suggesting Nugent was an immediate threat, while the BBC and NPR do not mention this detail.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · BBC · ABC News · NPR

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Gaza children face worsening food shortages as prices rise and aid is cut, threatening their health and survival.

Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in Gaza

The World Food Programme (WFP) has scaled back its aid to Gaza, reducing support from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people each month. This follows a more than 50% drop in funding from 2025 levels. The WFP’s director for Palestine, Shaun Hughes, warned that the situation remains dire, with two-thirds of the population facing crisis levels of food insecurity. The agency needs over £300m over six months to maintain its programmes. Food insecurity is at emergency levels for 200,000 Palestinians, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). The WFP has also reduced food rations and hot meals, with deliveries now occurring every other day in October. Most families in Gaza still rely on aid due to high unemployment, with about 80% of the population unemployed, according to UN data.

Gaza’s agricultural and fishing sectors have been severely impacted, with farmland occupied by Israeli forces and fishing boats barred from coastal waters. A recent Unicef survey found that one in eight children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted. Humanitarian organisations are struggling with funding after the Trump administration cut USAID and donor nations reduced aid due to cost of living crises. Aid will be needed until Israel and the international community launch promised reconstruction efforts.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the WFP reduced support from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people in October, while Al Jazeera states that the WFP cut support from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October. The Guardian attributes the reduction to funding cuts, while Al Jazeera notes that the WFP cited funding shortages as the reason for the cuts. The Guardian mentions that the famine declared in summer 2025 has receded, while Al Jazeera states that famine was declared in Gaza City in August 2025 and that the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification indicated it had receded after the ceasefire began in June 2025. The Guardian attributes the reduction in hot meals to funding cuts, while Al Jazeera specifies that the WFP halved food rations and reduced hot meals from 250,000 to 150,000 daily.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera

France Faces Widespread Protests, Riots, and Government Crackdown

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the "unbridled violence" during nationwide protests that turned into riots, with public buildings burned, shops looted, and thousands arrested. The unrest began as student-led demonstrations over school conditions but expanded to include concerns about the cost of living and fuel prices. Macron blamed the violence on an "ultra-left movement" and vowed to hold those responsible accountable. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also accused the "ultra-left movement" of orchestrating disorder ahead of the presidential election. The government imposed curfews in several cities, including Paris, Nice, and Lyon, and warned of potential national emergency measures. The protests have also drawn international attention, with U.S. politicians like Donald Trump and JD Vance blaming mass migration for the unrest.

Where the accounts differ

The Free Press and The Guardian both mention the protests began as student-led demonstrations over school conditions, but The Free Press characterizes the protests as "school protests" and criticizes the French government's education spending, while The Guardian does not mention education spending. The Guardian reports that the protests started as peaceful demonstrations over school conditions and the cost of living, but does not attribute the violence to any specific group. FOX News and The New York Post both attribute the violence to "ultra-left" groups and link the protests to broader political movements, while The Guardian does not mention any specific political groups. The New York Post and FOX News both claim that the protests have been linked to "open borders" and mass migration, while The Guardian does not mention immigration as a factor. The Guardian reports that the protests have caused a debt sell-off and increased borrowing costs, while The Free Press and The New York Post do not mention financial impacts.

Sources The Free Press · FOX News · New York Post · Just The News · The Guardian · CBS News

Trump Plows Forward With Plan to Build the Golf Course of His Dreams in DC

President Donald Trump announced plans to shut down the East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, DC, for 15 months to remodel it into a facility capable of hosting international golf competitions. Construction is set to begin on November 15, according to a post on Truth Social. The National Park Service has been cutting down hundreds of trees at the course, which they claim is part of a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report to restore the site. However, a federal judge, Ana C. Reyes, has temporarily halted additional tree removal, citing concerns over the timing and lack of notice. Trump has also faced legal challenges over the project, with a judge criticizing the government for acting hastily and suggesting the tree removal was connected to his renovation plans.

The project has drawn criticism from preservation groups and local officials, who argue that the course is a historic public space and that Trump’s plans could displace long-time users and alter the character of the area. The National Park Service and the Department of the Interior have been involved in the planning, with golf architect Tom Fazio working on the redesign. Trump has described the existing course as "old, broken, dilapidated," and has claimed the renovation will create jobs and boost the local economy.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones states that the National Park Service began cutting trees earlier this month as part of a 2019 restoration plan, while FOX News and The Guardian report that the tree removal occurred over Columbus Day weekend, with more than 500 trees felled. The Guardian and NPR mention that the government was ordered to give notice before any substantial construction, which they failed to do, leading to a court-ordered halt. Newsweek and The Guardian note that Trump referred to the course as "Trash Island," a term not mentioned in Mother Jones or FOX News. The Washington Examiner reports that Judge Reyes withdrew her order requiring the DOJ to refile a brief with the names of career attorneys, a detail not included in other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · Washington Examiner · FOX News · Newsweek · The Guardian · NPR

Alberta voters reject separation from Canada in referendum

Alberta residents voted in a nonbinding referendum on Monday, deciding whether to begin the legal process toward a future independence referendum. The vote, described by Elections Alberta as the largest electoral event in the province's history, did not determine immediate separation but would allow for a future binding referendum. The results showed a majority of voters supported remaining in Canada. The referendum included 10 questions, with the final one asking whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or start the legal process for a separation referendum. The vote was called by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who opposed separation but believed the process would allow residents to express their views.

The referendum has been shaped by long-standing tensions between Alberta and Ottawa, particularly over energy policy and economic control. Separatists argue that Alberta's oil wealth is unfairly managed by the federal government, while opponents warn of the economic and political instability that could result from separation. The vote also occurred amid a deadly fire at a military base in CFB Wainwright, which affected the campaign's momentum.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the referendum was called after pressure from within the United Conservative Party and that Premier Danielle Smith estimated the cost of separation at C$400bn for transition and C$25bn-$50bn annually. The BBC states that a court blocked the pro-separation petition for not consulting First Nations, and that Smith's decision to proceed was criticized as "undemocratic" by First Nations groups. Al Jazeera and CBS News both report early results showing about 76% of voters supported remaining in Canada, with 23% backing the process toward separation. The Guardian and NPR differ on the nature of the vote, with the Guardian describing it as a vote on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding independence referendum, while NPR clarifies it is a nonbinding referendum on whether to begin the legal process for a future independence referendum.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · BBC · NPR · Al Jazeera · CBS News

Musk pledges to give one SpaceX share to every child in America next year

Elon Musk announced Monday that he will give one SpaceX share to every child in the U.S. next year, calling it "the first of many." The pledge was made in a post on X, the social media platform Musk owns. Musk did not specify how the shares would be distributed or whether the giveaway would be limited to U.S. citizens or all children present in the country. The plan comes as part of the Trump Accounts program, which allows donors to contribute stock to children's investment accounts without paying capital-gains taxes. President Trump thanked Musk for the pledge, stating it aligns with the program's original vision.

The Trump Accounts program, which allows for stock donations, has already enrolled nearly 8 million children, with plans to add more than 60 million others through an auto-enrollment feature. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell previously announced that she and her husband would donate stock to Trump Accounts for over 2 million children. The Internal Revenue Service recently issued regulations to facilitate such donations.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Hill attribute the statement about Trump Accounts to President Trump, while Fox Business and CBS News do not explicitly attribute the statement to Trump. The Washington Examiner and The Hill report that Trump thanked Musk for the pledge, while Fox Business and CBS News mention Trump's gratitude but do not attribute the statement directly to him. The Newsweek article includes a calculation of the giveaway's value at $10.5 billion, which is also present in Axios and CBS News. The Axios article notes that Musk did not clarify whether "kid" refers to all minors under 18 or another status, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Axios · The Hill · Fox Business · Newsweek · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say

A Houthi missile strike hit a security training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, killing at least 50 recruits and injuring over 200, according to local authorities. The attack targeted the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from multiple provinces were being trained. The Houthis claimed the strike was aimed at "Saudi enemy concentrations" and said it resulted in the deaths of dozens of "Saudi enemy" forces, including officers. The Yemeni government condemned the attack as a "criminal attack" and called for a "firm response." The strike is among the deadliest since the recent escalation of the conflict.

The attack occurred amid ongoing fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis, with both sides intensifying attacks on each other's territory. The Houthis have been targeting Saudi infrastructure, including airports, while Saudi forces have launched airstrikes in Yemen. The Yemeni government has also accused the Houthis of fabricating media victories to cover up their military setbacks.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the attack killed 53 and injured over 200, while The Guardian states at least 53 were killed. The Guardian also notes that the attack was the largest single loss of life since the civil war reignited in September. FOX News and Al Jazeera do not specify the exact number of casualties. The Guardian and BBC attribute the claim of the attack being the largest since the war reignited, while FOX News and Al Jazeera do not mention this. The Guardian and BBC describe the training camp as a center for internal security forces, while FOX News and Al Jazeera refer to it as a site where recruits were being trained. The Guardian and BBC attribute the claim that the camp was not a military target to Yemen's government, while FOX News and Al Jazeera do not mention this.

Sources BBC · FOX News · Al Jazeera · The Hill · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Four dead and dozens wounded after major fire breaks out at Canadian military base

A fire broke out at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday, resulting in four deaths and dozens of injuries. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime. The fire spread rapidly due to strong winds, affecting soldiers engaged in live-fire training. Emergency services and medical teams responded swiftly, with multiple ambulances and air ambulances deployed to treat the injured.

The fire originated in a grassy training area and spread quickly, engulfing soldiers conducting high-intensity combat training with live munitions. Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the Edmonton-based 1st Canadian Division, stated that the fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted, which is not normal for a fire to move that distance in 36 seconds. The cause of the fire remains under investigation, though officials noted that the wind played a significant role in its rapid spread.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both report that the fire broke out at the base, but the Washington Examiner does not mention the specific training activities or the names of the deceased. The BBC and Al Jazeera provide detailed information about the training exercises and the names of the four soldiers who died. The Daily Caller mentions an explosion that may have triggered the fire, a claim not made by other outlets. The Straight Arrow News does not specify the cause of the fire or the names of the deceased, while the BBC and Al Jazeera attribute the fire's spread to wind and the training activities.

Sources Washington Examiner · BBC · Al Jazeera · Straight Arrow News · FOX News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Abdul El-Sayed Makes His Pitch To People Of Faith. Will Christians Buy It?

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, released a video in which he described himself as a man of faith who prays every day. The ad was released as President Trump criticized El-Sayed’s faith, calling him a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed’s campaign has stated he opposes incorporating any religion’s rules into U.S. law and has argued that his Muslim faith should not define his candidacy. In a town hall, El-Sayed faced a question from a man who identified himself as “Tommy,” asking him to disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed responded by questioning Tommy’s assumptions about his loyalty, comparing the situation to John F. Kennedy’s experience as a Catholic candidate. The exchange went viral and was widely shared on social media.

El-Sayed’s campaign has also highlighted endorsements from clergy across various religious traditions, including Rev. Shannon Jammal-Hollemans, who praised his leadership on health care. However, some religious leaders, like Pastor Lorenzo Sewell, have expressed skepticism about El-Sayed’s ability to represent Christian values in the Senate. El-Sayed’s campaign has also noted that his attention to how his religion appears on camera dates back to his gubernatorial campaign, where he instructed filmmakers to avoid showing religious items in his home.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News both mention that El-Sayed responded to a question from a man who identified himself as “Tommy,” but they differ on the nature of the exchange. The Daily Wire describes the interaction as a viral moment where El-Sayed questioned Tommy’s assumptions about his loyalty, while Straight Arrow News provides a more detailed account of the exchange, including specific questions El-Sayed asked Tommy. The Guardian and Mother Jones both mention that Tommy is a former Republican strategist, but the Guardian attributes this information to Marisa Kabas, while Mother Jones attributes it to The Handbasket. The Hill does not mention Tommy or the town hall exchange at all.

Sources The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · The Hill · The Guardian · Slate · Straight Arrow News

Macron says violent rioters will be ‘prosecuted and punished’ as buildings burn in France

French President Emmanuel Macron denounced violent rioters who attacked law enforcement and damaged national landmarks during escalating protests. The unrest, which began as student-led demonstrations over education policies, has expanded to include public sector workers and unions. Protests across France saw clashes between protesters and police, with some demonstrations turning violent as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted. The violence has drawn condemnation from government officials, who have called for accountability.

The protests, which began last month at schools in Paris, have grown into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending, and rising living costs. Demonstrators have called for higher wages, better pensions, and lower prices. While most marches were peaceful, violent groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques, and supermarkets, attacking police vehicles and officers. The government has reported hundreds of arrests and injuries to police officers.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and BBC both report that Macron condemned violent rioters and called for prosecution, but the Washington Examiner omits the specific details about the scale of the violence and the number of arrests. The Guardian and CBS News provide more specific numbers, with the Guardian reporting 1,200 arrests initially and later 1,800, while CBS News states 855 arrests. The Guardian also mentions the damage to the Limoges town hall, including the collapse of the roof, which CBS News and BBC also report. The Guardian and BBC both mention the involvement of the gilets jaunes movement, while the Washington Examiner does not. The FOX News account attributes the violence to "radical far-left groups" and mentions Macron's comments about political exploitation, which are not included in the other accounts. The NPR account includes quotes from protesters and union members, which are absent in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · NPR · CBS News · FOX News · BBC

GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers breaks with Trump over Russia sanctions — as retiring lawmakers lash president

Republican Michigan Senate hopeful Mike Rogers criticized President Trump over his decision to pause sanctions on Russia, arguing that the administration should enforce the bipartisan sanctions legislation. Rogers, who has generally aligned with Trump on policy, expressed skepticism that waiving the sanctions would lower diesel prices in the U.S. He also rejected claims that Trump is siding with Russia in its war against Ukraine, instead framing the move as an effort to address energy costs and confront Iran. Other Republicans, including retiring Senators, have also publicly challenged Trump’s decision to waive the Russia sanctions.

President Trump announced Friday that he was waiving sanctions under the Graham Act, a bipartisan measure aimed at punishing Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas. The legislation, named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, authorized tariffs of up to 100% on major importers of Russian petroleum products. Trump cited “national interests of the United States” as the rationale for the waiver, which drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties who accused the administration of giving Moscow a break.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and Axios both report that Trump waived sanctions under the Graham Act, while The Hill clarifies that no sanctions were lifted, only the diesel embargo. The New York Post and BBC describe Trump’s rationale as focusing on energy prices and negotiations with Russia, whereas Axios and The Hill note that Trump’s aides offered conflicting explanations for the move. The BBC and NPR report that Zelenskyy criticized the waiver as helping Russia in its war against Ukraine, while the New York Post and Straight Arrow News attribute similar statements to Zelenskyy. The Straight Arrow News and NPR also report that Zelenskyy described the attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as one of the country’s largest, while the BBC and Axios provide more detail on the nature of the attack.

Sources New York Post · NPR · Straight Arrow News · BBC · Axios · The Hill

Trump Plows Forward With Plan to Build the Golf Course of His Dreams in DC

President Donald Trump announced plans to shut down the East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, DC, for 15 months to renovate it into a facility capable of hosting international golf tournaments. The project, which he described as “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World,” would begin on November 15. Trump did not specify the cost or funding for the project. The National Park Service had previously started cutting down hundreds of trees at the course, citing a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report to restore the site. However, a federal judge, Ana C. Reyes, issued a temporary restraining order halting further tree removal, citing the government’s late notice and what she called “raced to undertake” actions due to Trump’s demands for haste. The Justice Department has requested that Reyes be removed from the case, accusing her of “bias.”

The renovation has faced legal challenges, with plaintiffs arguing that the project would alter the character of the space and make it less affordable to the public. Democracy Forward, representing the plaintiffs, stated that the course is part of a national park and recreation facility meant for everyone. The Trump administration has also faced criticism for removing over 400 trees from the site, which was part of a 2019 plan predating Trump’s ambitions for the course. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Monday.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Guardian both note that the National Park Service began cutting trees in accordance with a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report, while FOX News and the New York Post describe the tree removal as part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump’s ambitions. The Guardian and NPR mention that the Trump administration asked Judge Reyes to dismiss the litigation, stating the project was at an early conceptual stage, while the New York Post and Washington Examiner do not mention this request. The Guardian and FOX News report that Trump did not acknowledge the legal fight in his post, while Mother Jones and NPR note that Trump made no mention of the legal battle in his Truth Social post. The New York Post and FOX News include details about the number of trees cut down (430) and the timing of the tree removal (just before Columbus Day weekend), which are not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · The Guardian · NPR · Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post

Kansas driver who allegedly killed two and hurt 10 at soccer game is released from custody

A woman arrested after driving a truck through a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, has been released from custody without charges. The incident occurred on Saturday afternoon at the Stryker Sports Complex, where the driver struck and killed a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man. Ten others were injured, with five of them being children. The driver, identified as a 34-year-old woman from Garden City, Kansas, was in police custody but later released pending toxicology and mechanical examination results. Authorities have not confirmed whether the crash was intentional or due to any medical condition or impairment.

The driver had two of her children in the truck at the time of the incident, and a third child was playing soccer elsewhere at the complex. Emergency responders arrived at the scene shortly after 3:25 p.m. CT, where bystanders had already begun providing aid to the injured. The victims included several children and adults, with injuries described as traumatic but not life-threatening. The McPherson City FC youth soccer club expressed deep sorrow over the deaths of two of its members, calling the incident an "unimaginable tragedy."

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and FOX News both mention that the driver had two children in the truck, while Straight Arrow News and CBS News refer to them as "juveniles." The Guardian and FOX News state that the driver was released pending toxicology and mechanical examination results, while The Daily Wire and ABC News mention that the driver was released after consulting with the district attorney’s office. The Guardian and FOX News provide specific names of the victims, Cole Adrian and Nicholas Schafer, while The Daily Wire and ABC News also identify them by name. The Guardian and FOX News note that the driver had a valid license and no outstanding warrants, while The Daily Wire and ABC News do not mention this detail.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · Straight Arrow News · FOX News · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Massachusetts GOP candidate Shawn Oliver arrested, suspends campaign

Shawn Oliver, a New Bedford City Council member and Republican candidate for Massachusetts lieutenant governor, was arrested and suspended his campaign following a late-night crash. The incident occurred around 11:40 p.m. on Dartmouth Street in New Bedford. Police reported that Oliver's SUV flipped over and collided with multiple parked cars, involving five vehicles. Two of these vehicles sustained extensive damage. Oliver was taken to St. Luke’s Hospital for treatment and later arrested on charges including operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, marked lanes violation, and speeding. Oliver suspended his campaign, stating the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue called for Oliver to suspend his campaign, expressing disappointment and emphasizing the need for accountability.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Hill both mention that Oliver was taken to St. Luke’s Hospital for treatment and that he was released around 9:30 a.m. Sunday. The Hill adds that he was released less than three hours after being booked. The New York Post states he was released from jail at around 9:30 a.m. and is set to be arraigned Monday. The Washington Examiner and Just The News do not mention the time of release. The New York Post also notes that Oliver’s wife said he was “very hurt” about the situation, a detail not included in other accounts. The Hill and CBS News report that Oliver was alone at the time of the crash and did not appear to be hurt, while the New York Post suggests he was injured.

Sources CBS News · Washington Examiner · Just The News · The Hill · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system still restricted in Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine's use of the Elon Musk-owned SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, limiting the military's ability to use drones for intercepting Russian attack drones and sending supplies to front-line soldiers. Zelensky noted that the restrictions appear to apply only within Ukraine, as the system functions normally in European Union countries. He expressed skepticism about SpaceX's claim that the speed limit results from technical problems, suggesting instead that the restrictions may stem from a political decision by the Trump administration. Zelensky also mentioned ongoing discussions with U.S. officials, including Jared Kushner, to resolve the issue.

U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and President Trump, have denied any involvement in restricting Ukraine's access to the Starshield system, which is controlled by the U.S. government. Trump claimed the service is fully operational, while Rubio stated that Ukraine has not had access to Starshield and that the system is a military product not available to Ukraine. Ukrainian officials, however, report that the system's speed limit has been reduced to 161 kilometers per hour, affecting drone operations within Ukraine.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Ukrainian officials are still determining whether the restrictions result from a political decision by the Trump administration or Musk, with conflicting claims from both sides. The New York Post notes that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Zelensky for publicly accusing the Trump administration of throttling Starshield, while Axios and CBS News describe Bessent's comments. The Hill and CBS News both mention Rep. Mike Turner calling for an investigation into the loss of Starlink access, though The Hill specifies that the speed limit was 100 mph, while Axios and CBS News report 161 km/h. The Daily Caller and The Hill both mention Turner's call for an investigation, but The Daily Caller adds that Turner cited reports from the Institute for the Study of War and Zelensky as evidence of spotty service.

Sources Axios · New York Post · The Hill · CBS News · NPR · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Trump endorses Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s elections, warns US will have to act alone if Israel fails

President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, urging Israeli voters to support him in the Oct. 27 Knesset elections. Trump called Netanyahu a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "Partner for Peace" in the fight against Iran, warning that if Israel selects a leader other than Netanyahu, the U.S. would have to "finish the job" against Iran alone. Netanyahu responded by thanking Trump for his support and stating that "Together, we will complete the mission."

The endorsement comes amid a closely contested election where Netanyahu’s Likud Party is projected to secure between 18–22 seats, while a Netanyahu-aligned right-religious bloc is expected to win around 49–51 seats — short of a majority. The Israeli elections will determine the next prime minister through a proportional representation system, with the Knesset’s 120 seats distributed among parties that clear the 3.25% threshold. Trump’s endorsement is seen as a significant boost for Netanyahu, who faces challenges from within Israel, including his ongoing corruption trial and public backlash over the handling of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and The Daily Wire both report that Trump called Netanyahu a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "Partner for Peace," and that Netanyahu responded by thanking Trump for his support. However, FOX News includes a quote from Netanyahu stating, "Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and the joint work," while The Daily Wire attributes the same statement to Netanyahu in a Hebrew post on X. The Daily Wire also includes a quote from Netanyahu saying, "Together we will complete the mission," which is not present in FOX News.

The New York Post and Axios both mention that Trump’s endorsement was made nine days before the election, but the New York Post adds that Netanyahu’s Likud Party is running behind Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar Party in several polls, while Axios notes that neither party is expected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority. The New York Post also includes details about Netanyahu’s declining popularity in Israel due to the conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, as well as his corruption trial and backlash over the Oct. 7 attack, which are not mentioned in Axios.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · Axios · The Daily Wire · NPR

Abdul El-Sayed Confronted Bigoted Question About Muslim Brotherhood at Town Hall

At a Michigan Senate town hall on Saturday, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed was asked by an audience member to disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed responded by questioning the implication of the question, comparing it to the religious bias faced by John F. Kennedy during his presidential campaign. The exchange, which was widely shared on social media, ended when the man, who identified himself as Tommy, refused to disavow the group and left the event. El-Sayed emphasized his commitment to protecting the right to practice faith, stating that he would not tell others what faith they could or could not practice. The incident has drawn attention to the ongoing targeting of El-Sayed over his Muslim faith, including past attacks by former President Donald Trump.

El-Sayed's response to the question was detailed in multiple accounts, with some noting that the man who asked the question was later identified as Thomas Teepell, who had previously worked for Senator Josh Hawley. The accounts also mention that El-Sayed's opponents, including former Rep. Mike Rogers, have made false claims about his ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which have been debunked by media outlets. The event has been framed as a moment where El-Sayed effectively countered Islamophobic rhetoric, with some outlets highlighting the broader implications of such questions in political discourse.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Hill both describe the event and El-Sayed's response, but Mother Jones provides additional context about Tommy's background, including his father's political connections and his ties to Christian Nationalist figures. The Hill, however, does not mention these details. The Hill also notes that there was no evidence of El-Sayed's ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, a point not included in Mother Jones. Mother Jones attributes the characterization of the question as Islamophobic to Soraya Nadia McDonald, while The Hill does not mention this characterization.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · FOX News

World Food Programme cuts aid to Gaza due to funding shortages

The World Food Programme (WFP) has announced it is forced to drastically reduce lifesaving assistance to Gaza due to funding shortages. The number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third, from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The cuts will hit as winter approaches, when many families in Gaza are already struggling to feed themselves. The number of hot meals provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day. Families in hard-to-reach areas will receive a meal every other day instead of daily. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced, with two-thirds relying on food aid to survive.

The WFP acting executive director, Carl Skau, described life in Gaza as "absolutely brutal," noting that basic services are lacking, there is massive destruction, and insecurity continues. He reported that the WFP has been reaching almost every person in Gaza for the past few months, but progress is fragile and could be reversed. Skau also mentioned that the WFP is cutting assistance because funding is no longer there, not because needs have decreased or access is limited.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the WFP is cutting assistance due to funding shortages, and that the number of people helped will drop from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. It also mentions that the WFP is cutting almost half a million people off assistance in the next few weeks. BBC states that the number of people helped will drop by about a third, from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, and that the number of hot meals provided will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day. NPR does not mention the reduction in hot meals, while BBC does. NPR also states that the WFP is cutting assistance because funding is no longer there, not because needs have decreased or access is limited. BBC states that the cuts are being made because of finances, not because the needs are coming down or because the WFP doesn't have access.

Sources NPR · BBC
